rv.q: The Lazours have crafted a piece that is long on emotion with melodies that can burn with revolutionary fervor, if at the expense of clarity and structural coherence.
But while passions supposedly run high, the temperature of this new musical — which at best and at worst feels like “Rent” on the barricades — almost never rises above tepid.
As a production, Cairo is highly impactful.
We Live in Cairo is an intensely sweet and powerful musical that focuses on the impact of revolution and upheaval on individual lives.
Nevertheless, this is the most interesting and accomplished new musical to come our way this season.
We Live in Cairo is replete with rousing choreography and movement direction by Ann Yee.
If “We Live in Cairo” is hardly a masterpiece, it deserves credit for honoring the real people, dead and living, who showed similar courage.
There is great value in the deep dive into Egyptian history and politics.

Yet in its inexpert mixing of the political and the personal, its plotlines that wander around and sometimes end up nowhere, it still seems that We Live in Cairo hasn't entirely dotted its alifs and crossed its taas.
The show’s unevenness is due in part to the performances.
With greater focus (and probably an outside pair of eyes to tighten things up), We Live in Cairo could be major; at this moment, it’s more respectable than truly enjoyable.
The score is a combination of western rock musical and Arab influences, and it is the most hypnotic and unique original score I’ve heard in a musical in a very long time.
But We Live in Cairo is trying to tell a story that doesn't actually have a nice tie-up ending, like the fiction that lives rent-free in Rent .
But despite all the polish, We Live in Cairo feels like a work in progress that hasn’t been so much completed as let go.

cn.t: An ambitious musical about Egypt's Arab Spring pulses with youthful energy and intelligence, though critics find the interpersonal drama less compelling than the political backdrop. Strong staging and an all-Arab cast earn praise.

vr.q: this is definitely one of the most exciting new scores I've encountered in a while
